exp: System 1 (public weather API) should be REST/JSON: third-party integrators, especially hobbyists, need to be able to call the API with a browser, curl, or a simple script in whatever language they have, with no protobuf toolchain or generated stubs required -- and call volume per integrator is low enough that JSON's verbosity and REST's lack of a strict schema are non-issues. System 2 (internal fleet) should be gRPC: all callers are internal teams that already have modern build tooling and can absorb a codegen step, the call volume (50,000/sec) is high enough that protobuf's smaller, faster-to-parse payloads and HTTP/2 multiplexing produce a real, measurable difference, and the compiled .proto contracts prevent the kind of silent schema drift that becomes increasingly costly to discover at runtime as the number of internal services and calls grows.

expl: The two systems differ on exactly the two axes that should drive this decision: who is calling, and how much. System 1's callers are external, numerous, tooling-constrained, and individually low-volume -- REST's universal accessibility (any HTTP client, human-readable payloads, zero required codegen) directly serves that population, and gRPC's performance advantage would be paid for by every one of those integrators in onboarding friction for a throughput benefit none of them individually need. System 2's callers are internal, few, tooling-capable, and collectively extremely high-volume -- gRPC's binary serialization and HTTP/2 multiplexing produce real savings at 50,000 calls/sec that would show up as measurable latency and CPU cost if paid in JSON-over-HTTP/1.1 instead, and every caller already has the engineering capacity to run a codegen step, so that cost is genuinely negligible for this population. Picking gRPC for System 1 or REST for System 2 would both be defensible-sounding but wrong choices, because each ignores the actual caller population in favor of a generic 'which protocol is better' framing.

expl: The root mistake is treating "gRPC is faster and more strictly typed" as a universal ranking rather than a tradeoff that depends on the caller -- and in this case, one of the actual callers is the team's own browser-based frontend, which structurally cannot speak native gRPC the way a backend service can, because browser networking APIs don't expose the HTTP/2 primitives gRPC needs. This isn't a performance problem to optimize away; it's a protocol mismatch that requires an architectural fix, not a faster gRPC implementation. The practical fix is to put a translation layer between the browser and the gRPC backend -- either a REST-to-gRPC gateway (a natural fit for an API gateway, since it's already the front door translating and routing anyway) or a grpc-web-compatible proxy -- so the browser talks a browser-compatible protocol while internal services still get gRPC's benefits for service-to-service calls. The broader lesson: choosing a protocol "because it's better" without checking whether every real caller can actually speak it is exactly the mistake the previous concept's "choose by caller, not by benchmark" framing is meant to prevent.

exp: Checkout latency becomes the SUM of four sequential network calls (490ms best case) instead of one in-process operation, and every one of those four hops is an independent point of failure that needs its own timeout and retry handling -- so worst-case latency (with retries) can balloon well past 490ms, and average latency is also worse than an in-process call chain would be, since network round trips are added at every step. Failure-handling complexity increases sharply: if charge-payment-service succeeds but reserve-inventory-service then fails, something has to explicitly reverse the charge (a compensating action) -- and because the four services are separate deployables with no shared transaction, that reversal logic has to be built and maintained explicitly, rather than relying on a single database transaction's all-or-nothing rollback the way one order-service handling everything in one transaction could.

Checkout flow, decomposed by verb, all synchronous:
  client -> validate-cart-service      (60ms)
         -> charge-payment-service      (300ms, calls an external payment processor)
         -> reserve-inventory-service   (80ms)
         -> send-confirmation-service   (50ms)
  Total: ~490ms IF every call succeeds on the first try, with NO retries

Each service is independently deployable and independently can fail,
timeout, or need a retry.
expl: This is the 'one service per verb' anti-pattern in its clearest form: an operation that used to be conceptually (and, in a single service, could be technically) atomic is spread across four independently-failing network calls chained together. Latency accumulates additively across the chain instead of staying at the cost of one in-process call sequence, and every hop introduces its own possible timeout, retry, and partial-failure scenario that has to be explicitly designed for -- most critically, the case where an earlier step (charging the card) succeeded but a later step (reserving inventory) failed, which requires a compensating transaction (refund/void the charge) that a single-transaction, single-service design would never need at all, since a database transaction failure there would simply roll back everything atomically. None of these four services can be meaningfully deployed, scaled, or reasoned about independently of the others for this flow, despite being separate deployables -- exactly the distributed-monolith symptom of paying distribution's overhead without collecting its benefits.

The fix denormalizes the specific fields needed into the orders-service's own data, captured once at order-placement time -- which is also, notably, more semantically correct, since an order confirmation should reflect the shipping address as it was when the order was placed, not wherever the customer currently lives. This removes the synchronous dependency entirely from the hot path; users-service can be fully down and order-detail pages keep working, because orders-service now genuinely owns everything it needs to serve that page.

exp: In the current setup, the entire system becomes unreachable from outside the moment the single gateway instance crashes, regardless of how healthy all 12 backend services are -- the gateway is a single point of failure sitting in front of everything, and its being 'just routing infrastructure' doesn't exempt it from the same single-machine failure argument that applies to any other single instance. In the alternative setup, losing one of N gateway instances only reduces total gateway capacity by roughly 1/N (assuming the load balancer's health checks detect and route around the failed instance), and the system stays fully reachable as long as at least one gateway instance is healthy -- this requires each gateway instance to be stateless (e.g., rate-limit counters and any session-like data externalized to a shared store) so that any instance can correctly handle any incoming request.

expl: A single gateway instance is exactly as much a single point of failure as a single backend server would be -- every one of the 12 backend services being perfectly healthy is irrelevant if nothing outside the network can reach the gateway that fronts all of them, because the gateway sits on the only path in. This directly reuses the vertical-vs-horizontal-scaling argument from the scaling fundamentals module: a gateway's importance to the system (it fronts everything) makes its own availability more critical, not less, so treating it as exempt from horizontal scaling and load balancing because it's 'infrastructure rather than a service' is exactly backwards. Making the gateway stateless and running a load-balanced pool of instances applies the same fix used for any other horizontally-scaled tier: any healthy instance can handle any request, so losing one instance degrades capacity proportionally instead of taking down access to the entire backend fleet.

The cache entry set at 09:59:00 doesn't expire until 10:01:00, so it's still a hit at 10:00:30, returning the old cached price even though the database was already updated to $50 at 10:00:00. 10:01:00 -> the entry has just expired (boundary case, next read after this point misses). 10:02:30 -> $50 (fresh). 09:59:00 - page read, price=$40 cached, TTL=120s (expires 10:01:00)
10:00:00 - admin updates price in database to $50 (no cache invalidation call made)
10:00:30 - user reads page
10:01:00 - cache entry from 09:59:00 expires
10:02:30 - user reads page
expl: Because there's no explicit invalidation on the write path, the cache has no way to learn that the price changed at 10:00:00 -- it will keep serving whatever it cached at 09:59:00 until that entry's own TTL clock runs out, completely independently of when (or whether) the underlying data changes. The entry set at 09:59:00 with a 120-second TTL expires at exactly 10:01:00, so the 10:00:30 read (before expiry) is a hit on stale data -- a full 30 seconds of customers could see the wrong price after a change already took effect. The 10:02:30 read happens well after expiry, so it's a normal cache-aside miss: read the database (now correctly $50), cache it, return it. This is exactly the scenario where a TTL-only strategy trades correctness for simplicity -- if this were pricing data where even a 60-90 second stale window were a real cost (customer complaints, incorrect checkouts), explicit invalidation in the admin update path would be necessary to close that gap.

expl: Write-through only keeps the cache coherent for writes that pass through the specific code path that was written to update both the database and the cache together -- it says nothing about writes that reach the same underlying data through a different path. The admin tool updates the same `permissions` table directly, through entirely different code, and has no idea the main application even has a cache, let alone a cache key naming scheme to invalidate. From the cache's perspective, nothing happened at revoke time; it keeps serving the pre-revocation permissions for up to the full 600-second TTL. This is the "second writer" problem: any code path -- a different service, an admin tool, a batch job, a direct database console session -- that can modify data without going through the caching logic will silently desynchronize the cache, and write-through alone cannot protect against writers it doesn't know exist. The real fix requires either making the admin tool aware of the cache (explicit invalidation from every writer) or, for anything this security-sensitive, treating a long TTL as an unacceptable risk on its own and shortening it dramatically as a bounded worst case, ideally alongside fixing the missing invalidation rather than as a substitute for it.

exp: Write throughput does not improve at all -- it's still bottlenecked at exactly the same single leader node's capacity, since every write still has to be accepted and processed there first regardless of how many replicas exist downstream. Read latency likely improves significantly, since reads that used to compete with writes for the leader's resources can now be served by the 10 replicas instead, freeing up the leader to focus on writes (which may even modestly help write throughput indirectly, by removing read contention -- but it doesn't raise the leader's fundamental write ceiling). If write throughput was the actual, primary bottleneck, this change addresses a problem the system didn't complain about (read latency) while leaving the real bottleneck (write capacity) essentially where it was.

BEFORE: 1 node (leader), write capacity saturated at 100%, read latency high due to
        read queries competing with writes for the same node's resources
AFTER:  1 leader + 10 read replicas, ALL writes still go through the single leader,

expl: Replication, no matter how many replicas you add, only distributes read traffic -- every replica is a full copy that must apply every write from the leader, so the total volume of writes flowing into the system is completely unaffected by replica count; the leader is still the sole node accepting and processing writes, at the same ceiling as before. This scenario is a direct instance of the read-bound vs. write-bound diagnostic: since the actual reported bottleneck was write throughput at 100% capacity, adding read replicas -- a tool that specifically helps read capacity and availability -- doesn't touch the actual constraint. The team may see some real, if secondary, improvement (less read/write resource contention on the leader could modestly help), but if writes need genuine additional capacity, the correct lever is sharding (splitting write load across multiple independently-writable nodes) or reducing write volume itself (batching, deferring non-critical writes), not more replicas.

expl: The uneven CPU load is very likely a symptom of the same root cause as the expensive query: because orders are sharded by order_id rather than customer_id, a single customer's orders are scattered essentially randomly across all 8 shards. Every "get all orders for customer X" query therefore has to fan out to all 8 shards and merge results, even though logically it only needs one customer's data -- this is expensive on its own (8x the work of a single-shard query, network overhead, merge logic), and if certain customers (e.g. high-order-volume business accounts) are queried disproportionately often, the specific shards holding pieces of their scattered data end up doing disproportionate extra fan-out work, which can plausibly show up as one shard running hotter than the others depending on access patterns. The fix re-keys sharding around the field the dominant query actually filters by -- customer_id -- so each customer's full order history lives on exactly one shard, turning the most common query back into a cheap single-shard lookup, and removing the fan-out tax entirely for that access pattern. This illustrates the general principle from the shard-key discussion: the right shard key is chosen to match your dominant query pattern, not just to distribute rows evenly -- a key that distributes rows evenly but doesn't align with real queries can still produce bad, uneven real-world load.

Cluster: N = 5 replicas total
Write: must be acknowledged by W = 3 replicas before returning success to the client
Read:  must be queried on R = 3 replicas, client takes the most recent value seen

Why W + R > N (3 + 3 = 6 > 5) guarantees the read sees the latest write:
  The write touched SOME set of 3 replicas out of 5.
  The read queries a DIFFERENT set of 3 replicas out of 5.
  Two sets of size 3, drawn from a pool of 5, MUST overlap by at least 1
  (3 + 3 = 6, which is more than the 5 available slots -- by the pigeonhole
   principle, they can't be fully disjoint).
  That guaranteed overlap of at least 1 replica has seen BOTH the write
  and is included in the read -- so the read is guaranteed to see the
  latest value (or something at least as recent) from that overlapping replica.

SYNCHRONOUS replication (leader waits for follower ack before confirming to client):
  Client write -> Leader -> [wait for Follower ack] -> Leader confirms to client
  Write latency: leader's write time + full round trip to follower + follower's write time
  Consistency: strong, for that follower -- a read reaching it right after is guaranteed current
  Cost: if the follower is slow, down, or unreachable (partition), the write STALLS or fails
        -> this IS the CAP tradeoff, made concrete: consistency purchased with availability

ASYNCHRONOUS replication (leader confirms immediately, replicates in background):
  Client write -> Leader -> Leader confirms to client immediately
                          -> (separately, in the background) Leader -> Follower
  Write latency: just the leader's own write time -- fast, unaffected by follower health
  Consistency: eventual -- follower catches up "soon," but a read hitting it right after

The transactional outbox pattern closes that gap by making the event a row in the *same database transaction* as the order itself: since both inserts are part of one transaction, either both are committed (order exists AND its outbox event is recorded, ready to be published) or neither is (a rolled-back transaction has no order and no dangling outbox row either) -- there is no longer a window where one exists without the other. A separate relay process then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, retrying on failure; because this relay step is itself only guaranteed at-least-once, the outbox row is only marked published after a successful publish, and any consumer of order_placed still needs to be idempotent in case the relay publishes the same row more than once during a retry.

Because both are on the same synchronous path, any slowness or transient failure in the analytics table -- a concern totally unrelated to whether the redirect itself is healthy -- directly degrades or breaks the redirect response, which is exactly the outcome observed.    because both nodes independently serve read traffic, so if one node is slow, the
   other answers instead. This holds under all failure conditions, including a
   network partition between Node A and Node B."
expl: The flawed claim is "guarantees both, under all failure conditions, including a network partition" -- that's precisely the combination CAP proves impossible to sustain once a partition is real. "Synchronously confirmed on both nodes" is exactly the mechanism that becomes impossible during a partition: if Node A cannot reach Node B, it cannot synchronously confirm anything with it, no matter how carefully the synchronization code is written -- this isn't a bug better code could fix, it's a hard consequence of the message simply not being deliverable. So during a real partition, the system has to do one of two things: refuse to confirm the write until it can reach Node B again (sacrificing availability, becoming CP for that operation), or confirm the write locally anyway and reconcile later (sacrificing strict consistency, becoming AP for that operation). Advertising both simultaneously as guaranteed "under all failure conditions" is a claim no implementation can honestly make; the fix is to be explicit about which guarantee bends during a partition, which is exactly the kind of decision a system-design review should force into the open before it's discovered in production during a real incident.

code:
Corrected claim:
  "During normal operation (no partition), writes are synchronously confirmed on
   both Node A and Node B, guaranteeing strong consistency, and both nodes serve
   reads, giving high availability.

   During a network partition between Node A and Node B, we choose consistency
   over availability: a node that cannot reach its peer to synchronously confirm
   a write will reject that write (or reject reads it cannot guarantee are current)
   rather than risk serving or accepting an inconsistent value. This is a CP system,
   not a CA system -- availability is intentionally sacrificed during a partition
   to preserve correctness."
